parts.display_text: A nearby star is 79 light-years from the Sun. Estimate its total apparent angular shift in degrees between observations from opposite points of Earth’s orbit, six months apart. Use 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m and 1 light-year = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m. Neglect the star’s own motion.

answer.text: The baseline is 2 AU. The total shift is θ ≈ 2 AU/d = 3.00 × 10¹¹/(79 × 9.46 × 10¹⁵) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ rad = 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ degrees.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Consider the net fusion of two deuterium nuclei into a helium-4 nucleus, with released energy carried away as radiation. Their nuclear masses are m_D = 2.013553 u and m_He = 4.001505 u. Calculate the energy released in forming 1.00 mol of helium-4. Use 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

answer.text: Mass decrease per reaction: Δm = 2(2.013553) − 4.001505 = 0.025601 u. Energy per helium nucleus = 0.025601 × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 3.82 × 10⁻¹² J. For one mole, E = 3.82 × 10⁻¹² × 6.02 × 10²³ = 2.30 × 10¹² J.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.display_text:
Three stationary helium-4 nuclei fuse into one carbon-12 nucleus and two gamma photons. One helium nucleus has mass 6.645×10⁻²⁷ kg and one carbon nucleus has mass 1.993×10⁻²⁶ kg. The energy released is closest to

A. 5.0×10⁻³⁰ J
B. 1.5×10⁻²¹ J
C. 4.5×10⁻¹³ J
D. 1.2×10⁻⁹ J

answer.text: Official key C checked; editorial worked explanation: Δm=3(6.645×10⁻²⁷)−1.993×10⁻²⁶≈5×10⁻³⁰ kg, so E=Δmc²=4.5×10⁻¹³ J.

evidence.detail: Official VCAA 2022 NHT report checked for Section A Question 11; explanation is editorial.

cross-ed24u5-7:whole.hint: Check which way surface temperature increases on the horizontal axis before locating the star.
notes: On a standard H–R diagram luminosity increases upwards and temperature increases to the left. Red giants are luminous but cool; white dwarfs are hot but faint.
Use L = 4πR²σT⁴ to compare radii. A hotter star is not necessarily more luminous, because emitting area also matters.

cross-aq24p2-17:whole.hint: Consider both the repulsion between nuclei and the chance of collisions while the fuel is confined.
notes: Fusion combines light nuclei into more tightly bound products. High temperature helps nuclei approach, high density increases collision rates, and confinement time allows reactions to occur.
Energy release comes from the mass difference or increase in total binding energy. High temperature is a condition for fusion; it is not the source of the released nuclear energy.

cross-ca24m4-written-10ai:whole.hint: Use the whole radiating surface area of the star.
notes: A spherical star radiates over 4πr², not its projected disc area πr². Luminosity is total power, whereas apparent brightness is power per unit area at the observer.

cross-aq24astro-written-2.1:whole.hint: The two observations are separated by a diameter of Earth’s orbit.
notes: IB’s stellar parallax angle p uses a 1 AU baseline and is half the total six-month angular shift. This question asks for the full shift; distinguish θ = 2p before calculating.

cross-aq24astro-written-3.2:whole.hint: Combine the star’s radiating surface area with the power emitted per unit area.
notes: The temperature result from the original spectrum question is supplied. Use r² and T⁴ carefully; luminosity uses the whole spherical surface.

cross-ca25n42-written-9-b:whole.hint: First calculate the mass decrease for a single reaction. Only then scale from one helium nucleus to a mole.
notes: The reaction consumes two deuterium nuclei for every helium nucleus, so include both reactant masses. Keep the full mass values until after subtraction.

cross-ca25n42-written-9-ci-cii:whole.hint: Convert the mass loss per second into energy released per second. Then relate total radiated power to surface area.
notes: Luminosity is total emitted power, in watts. The emitting area of a spherical star is 4πr², not the projected disc area πr².
Take the fourth root only after dividing by the entire denominator. This model assumes the stated mass loss is conversion to radiated energy rather than ejected matter.

cross-ca25m42-written-10-biii:whole.hint: Relate luminosity to the entire emitting surface area, then rearrange before taking the fourth root.
notes: A spherical star radiates over area 4πR². Its projected disc area πR² is not the emitting area in this calculation.

cross-fast-production-007-a-a11:whole.hint: Find initial minus final nuclear mass, then convert the positive mass defect with E=Δmc².
notes: Keep all masses in kilograms before subtracting because the defect is small.
